name: rco-concepts
note: Concept labels for the RCO classifier (card 1338 v1; card 1352 v2). ids are stable. A changed definition bumps the minor version. adding concepts bumps the minor version; this file is 2.0.0 because the schema gained status, aliases, and dropped records. A concept is never removed: mark it dropped instead, with dropped_reason, evidence, dropped_on, and revisit_when. A renamed concept keeps the old id as dropped. status is trained (has labels), untrained (listed, no labels yet), or dropped (kept as a deliberate decision, not a gap). aliases are optional synonyms for lookup before adding a concept. names and imports are lowercase hint tokens used only for trained concepts: names feed auto labels and the name signal, imports feed the import-lexicon signal. Labels and the baseline run stay on taxonomy version 1.0.0 until they are redone; v2 is a superset.

concepts.definition: Presentation for humans: terminal rendering, formatting, HTML templates, widgets.

concepts.definition: Durable storage access: databases, ORM, files used as stores, migrations.
concepts.source: PoEAA, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002): Data Source Architectural Patterns

concepts.definition: Domain model: the core entities and rules of the problem the software solves.
concepts.source: PoEAA, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002): Domain Model; Domain-Driven Design (2003)

concepts.definition: Configuration: loading, merging and validating settings, defaults, environment.
concepts.source: SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Construction: construction for configurability

concepts.definition: File system and stream input/output: reading, writing, paths, archives.

concepts.definition: Test code: unit, integration and acceptance tests, fixtures and test helpers.
Build, packaging of this repo, release, CI and developer scripts.

concepts.definition: General helpers with no single domain: utilities, compatibility glue, small helpers.
concepts.source: SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Construction: construction for reuse

concepts.definition: Operating-system integration: processes, signals, environment, platform detection.

concepts.definition: Factory Method or Abstract Factory: an object or function that decides which concrete class to create.
concepts.source: GoF, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994): Factory Method, Abstract Factory

concepts.definition: Adapter: converts one interface into another the caller expects (transport adapters, backends).
concepts.source: GoF, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994): Adapter

concepts.definition: Observer: subscribers are notified of events through signals, hooks, callbacks or listeners.
concepts.source: GoF, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994): Observer

concepts.definition: Strategy: interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, chosen at run time.
concepts.source: GoF, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994): Strategy

concepts.definition: Decorator: wraps an object or function to add behaviour without changing it.
concepts.source: GoF, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994): Decorator

concepts.definition: Command: requests packaged as objects (named commands, actions, undo, tasks).
concepts.source: GoF, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994): Command

concepts.definition: Visitor: an operation applied across a structure of nodes, as in tree or AST walkers.
concepts.source: GoF, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994): Visitor

concepts.definition: Chain of Responsibility: a request passes along a chain of handlers, as in middleware.
concepts.source: GoF, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994): Chain of Responsibility

concepts.definition: Proxy: a stand-in object that controls access to another, such as lazy or context-local proxies.
concepts.source: GoF, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994): Proxy

concepts.definition: Iterator: sequential access to elements of a collection without exposing its structure.
concepts.source: GoF, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994): Iterator

concepts.definition: Repository: a collection-like interface over stored domain objects, hiding the data source.
concepts.source: PoEAA, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002): Repository; Domain-Driven Design (2003)

concepts.definition: Pipes and Filters: data flows through a sequence of independent processing stages.
concepts.source: POSA vol. 1, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture: A System of Patterns (1996): Pipes and Filters

concepts.definition: Plugin or Microkernel: extensions discovered and loaded at run time through a defined extension point.
concepts.source: PoEAA, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002): Plugin; POSA vol. 1, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture: A System of Patterns (1996): Microkernel

concepts.definition: Model-View-Controller and web application structure: controllers or views over models with templates.
concepts.source: POSA vol. 1, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture: A System of Patterns (1996): Model-View-Controller

concepts.definition: Dependency injection: components receive collaborators from outside rather than constructing them.
concepts.source: "Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern" (2004 article)

concepts.definition: Messaging: asynchronous exchange through queues, brokers, channels or pub/sub.
Client-server split: client libraries and server implementations of a protocol.
concepts.source: POSA vol. 1, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture: A System of Patterns (1996): Broker; SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Architecture: architectural styles

concepts.definition: Interfaces and abstract types: abstract base classes, protocols, typed contracts between parts.
concepts.source: UML 2.5.1 (OMG 2017): Interface (10.4); Object-Oriented Software Construction, 2nd ed. (1997): Design by Contract

concepts.definition: Value objects and data classes: immutable or plain data carriers with structural equality.
State machines: explicit states and transitions driving behaviour.
Class hierarchies: base classes with specialised subclasses that override behaviour.
concepts.source: UML 2.5.1 (OMG 2017): Generalization (9.9); SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Design: object-oriented design

concepts.definition: Authentication and authorization: credentials, logins, tokens, permissions.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Security and privacy / Authentication; Access control

concepts.definition: Security mechanisms other than login: hashing, signing, TLS, sandboxing, CSRF.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Security and privacy / Security services

concepts.definition: Logging and diagnostics: log records, handlers, tracing, debug output, telemetry.
concepts.source: SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Maintenance: maintainability support

concepts.definition: Error handling: exception types, error mapping, recovery.
concepts.source: SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Construction: error handling, exception handling and fault tolerance

concepts.definition: Concurrency: threads, processes, async IO, event loops, locks, workers, schedulers.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Computing methodologies / Concurrent computing methodologies

concepts.definition: Caching: storing computed or fetched results for reuse, with keys and invalidation.
concepts.source: PoEAA, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002): Identity Map; SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Construction: performance

concepts.definition: Validation and contracts at the boundary: checking input against schemas or rules.
Compatibility and portability shims across Python versions, platforms or dependency versions.
Text encoding and internationalisation: charsets, unicode handling, locale.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Software and its engineering / Software notations and tools (character encodings)

concepts.definition: Lexical analysis: turning characters into tokens.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Software and its engineering / Compilers / Parsers (lexical analysis)

concepts.definition: Parsing: turning tokens or text into structured trees by grammar rules.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Software and its engineering / Compilers / Parsers

concepts.definition: Syntax trees and intermediate representations: node types and tree utilities.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Software and its engineering / Compilers / Intermediate representations

concepts.definition: Code generation, compilation and interpretation: emitting or running code from a tree or template.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Software and its engineering / Compilers / Code generation; Interpreters

concepts.definition: HTTP protocol handling: requests, responses, headers, cookies, status, multipart.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Networks / Network protocols / Application layer protocols

concepts.definition: Transport and connections: sockets, TLS streams, connection pools, proxies, DNS.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Networks / Network protocols / Transport protocols

concepts.definition: Client side of a protocol: code that issues requests to remote services.
concepts.source: SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Architecture: client-server style

concepts.definition: Server side of a protocol: listening, accepting and serving requests.
concepts.source: SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Architecture: client-server style

concepts.definition: Serialization: encoding and decoding data to and from wire or file formats (JSON, YAML, TOML, pickle).
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Information systems / Data management systems / Data structures (data exchange formats)

concepts.definition: Data structures: containers, mappings, trees, graphs and their algorithms.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Theory of computation / Design and analysis of algorithms / Data structures design and analysis

concepts.definition: Machine learning and numeric models: training, inference, model definitions, LLM calls.
concepts.source: ACM CCS 2012: Computing methodologies / Machine learning

concepts.definition: Version control integration: reading or driving git, hg or svn.
concepts.source: SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Configuration Management: software configuration control

concepts.definition: Package and dependency management as the product: resolving, installing, publishing packages.
concepts.source: SWEBOK v4 (IEEE CS 2024), Software Configuration Management: software building and release

concepts.definition: builder: constructs a complex object step by step so the same process can yield different representations.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: builder

concepts.definition: prototype: creates new objects by copying a typical instance rather than subclassing a constructor.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: prototype

concepts.definition: singleton: a class with a single shared instance and a global access point.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: singleton

concepts.definition: bridge: splits an abstraction from its implementations so the two can vary independently.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: bridge

concepts.definition: composite: treats individual objects and trees of objects through one uniform interface.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: composite

concepts.definition: facade: a single, simpler interface over a set of interfaces in a subsystem.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: facade

concepts.definition: flyweight: shares fine-grained state that many objects can reuse to cut memory use.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: flyweight

concepts.definition: interpreter: represents a grammar and an interpreter that evaluates sentences in that grammar.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: interpreter

concepts.definition: mediator: objects collaborate through a mediator object instead of referring to each other directly.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: mediator

concepts.definition: memento: captures and restores an object's internal state without exposing its structure.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: memento

concepts.definition: state: an object changes its behaviour when its internal state changes, as if its class had changed.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: state

concepts.definition: template method: a skeleton algorithm in a base type, with some steps deferred to subclasses or hooks.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns (gof), 1994: template method

concepts.definition: transaction script: organises business logic by procedure, one per request or transaction.
concepts.source: fowler, patterns of enterprise application architecture (poeaa), 2003: transaction script

concepts.definition: table module: one instance handles the business logic for all rows in a database table.
service layer: a layer of application services that sets the boundary and available operations.
table data gateway: an object that acts as a gateway to a database table, one instance per table.
row data gateway: an object that acts as a gateway to a single record in a data source.
active record: a domain object that wraps a row and includes the database access for that row.
data mapper: a layer that moves data between objects and a database while keeping them independent.
unit of work: keeps a list of objects affected by a business transaction and writes the changes together.
identity map: ensures each object is loaded only once per session by keeping a map of loaded records.
lazy load: defers loading an object's data until it is needed, often via a virtual proxy or ghost.
identity field: saves a database identity field in an object to maintain identity between memory and storage.
foreign key mapping: maps an object association to a foreign key reference in the database.
association table mapping: saves a many-to-many association as a table of pairs of foreign keys.
dependent mapping: has one class perform the database mapping for a child or dependent class.
embedded value: maps an object into several fields of another object's table row.
serialized lob: saves a graph of objects by serialising it into a single large object in the database.
single table inheritance: represents an inheritance hierarchy of classes as one table with a type column.
class table inheritance: represents an inheritance hierarchy with one table per class.
concrete table inheritance: represents an inheritance hierarchy with one table per concrete class.
inheritance mappers: a structure to organise database mappers that share mapping behaviour for a hierarchy.
metadata mapping: holds the object-relational mapping in metadata so general code can perform it.
query object: an object that represents a database query and can be built and composed in memory.
page controller: an object that handles a request for a specific page or action on a website.
front controller: a single handler that receives every request and then dispatches to the right command.
template view: renders a page by filling markers in an html or text template with information from objects.
transform view: renders a domain view by transforming a domain-oriented representation, often with xslt-style rules.
two step view: turns domain data into a logical page, then renders that logical page into html.
application controller: a centralised point for handling screen navigation and the flow of an application.
remote facade: a coarse-grained facade over fine-grained objects to cut the cost of remote calls.
data transfer object: an object that carries data between processes to reduce the number of remote calls.
optimistic offline lock: prevents conflicts between concurrent business transactions by detecting collisions on commit.
pessimistic offline lock: prevents conflicts by allowing only one business transaction at a time to access data.
coarse-grained lock: locks a set of related objects with a single lock, often on a root object.
implicit lock: lets framework or layer code acquire offline locks so application writers do not forget them.
client session state: stores session state on the client, for example in a cookie or hidden fields.
server session state: stores session state on the server in a memory or serialized session store.
database session state: stores session state as committed data in the database.
gateway: an object that encapsulates access to an external system or resource.
mapper: an object that sets up communication between two independent objects, often domain and database.
layer supertype: a type that acts as the common supertype for all types in its layer.
separated interface: defines an interface in a separate package from its implementation.
registry: a well-known object that other objects can use to find common objects and services.
money: represents a monetary value with a currency, avoiding raw floating-point arithmetic.
special case: a subclass that provides special behaviour for particular cases, including a null object.
service stub: removes dependence on a remote or awkward service during testing or development.
record set: an in-memory representation of tabular data, typically the result of a database query.
layered architecture: responsibilities are grouped into stacked layers, each talking mainly to its neighbours.
concepts.source: buschmann et al., pattern-oriented software architecture (posa), 1996: layers

concepts.definition: hexagonal architecture: the application core is reached only through ports, with adapters outside.
onion architecture: domain at the centre, with infrastructure and ui depending inward on interfaces.
clean architecture: use cases and entities at the centre, with interface adapters and frameworks outside.
event sourcing: state is the fold of a stored sequence of domain events, not a mutable record only.
cqrs: separate models for commands that change state and queries that read it.
broker: distributed components interact through a broker that locates, forwards and marshals requests.
blackboard: specialised knowledge sources cooperate by reading and writing a shared blackboard of partial results.
event-driven architecture: components react to events rather than to direct synchronous calls.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, enterprise integration patterns, 2003; common architectural style

concepts.definition: microservices: independently deployable services organised around business capabilities, communicating over a network.
concepts.source: lewis and fowler, microservices, 2014; newman, building microservices

concepts.definition: modular monolith: a single deployable unit with strict module boundaries and few, explicit dependencies.
monolith: a single deployable unit that owns many capabilities, without a required module split.
service-oriented architecture: capabilities are exposed as services with explicit contracts and composition.
concepts.source: open group soa source book / common soa literature

concepts.definition: rest: a style for networked systems based on resources, uniform interfaces and stateless interactions.
concepts.source: fielding, architectural styles and the design of network-based software architectures, 2000

concepts.definition: peer-to-peer: nodes act as both clients and servers and share work or data without a single central server.
space-based architecture: processing units share state through a distributed tuple or data space.
concepts.source: posa and related space-based / tuple-space styles

concepts.definition: serverless: application units are event-invoked functions or managed services, without a long-lived server process you operate.
lambda architecture: a batch layer and a speed layer together serve views over an append-only master dataset.
kappa architecture: a single stream-processing path over an append-only log, without a separate batch layer.
saga: a long-lived business transaction is a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions on failure.
concepts.source: garcia-molina and salem, sagas, 1987; richardson, microservices patterns

concepts.definition: strangler fig: a new system gradually wraps and replaces an old one, route by route, until the old one can go.
api gateway: a single entry in front of services for routing, auth, rate limits and protocol translation.
backend for frontend: a backend tailored to one client or user experience, rather than a one-size api.
sidecar: a companion process beside an application that adds platform features such as proxying or telemetry.
ambassador: a helper proxy for outbound calls, often for discovery, retries, or tls, without changing the app.
concepts.source: azure architecture center / cloud design patterns: ambassador

concepts.definition: service mesh: a dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service traffic, policy and observability.
model-view-presenter: the presenter updates the view through an interface and handles user actions.
model-view-viewmodel: a view-model exposes state and commands that a view binds to, often automatically.
presentation-abstraction-control: a tree of cooperating agents, each with presentation, abstraction and control.
read model: a query-side projection maintained for reads, separate from the write model.
message channel: a virtual pipe between a sender and a receiver of messages.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, enterprise integration patterns (eip), 2003: message channel

concepts.definition: message: a discrete unit of data sent on a channel, with a header and a body.
message router: consumes a message from one channel and republishes it to a chosen channel, without changing it.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: message router

concepts.definition: message translator: changes the content or format of a message so the receiver can understand it.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: message translator

concepts.definition: message endpoint: connects an application to a messaging channel so it can send and receive.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: message endpoint

concepts.definition: point-to-point channel: a channel that delivers each message to exactly one consumer.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: point-to-point channel

concepts.definition: publish-subscribe channel: a channel that delivers a copy of each message to every subscriber.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: publish-subscribe channel

concepts.definition: datatype channel: a dedicated channel for one type of data, so the receiver knows what to expect.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: datatype channel

concepts.definition: invalid message channel: a channel for messages that a receiver cannot process.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: invalid message channel

concepts.definition: dead letter channel: a channel for messages that the messaging system cannot deliver.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: dead letter channel

concepts.definition: guaranteed delivery: persists a message so it is not lost if the process or connection fails.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: guaranteed delivery

concepts.definition: channel adapter: connects an application's api or file or database to a messaging channel.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: channel adapter

concepts.definition: messaging bridge: connects messaging systems so messages from one can reach the other.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: messaging bridge

concepts.definition: message bus: a common communication spine and canonical format that participating applications share.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: message bus

concepts.definition: command message: a message that asks the receiver to run a given action.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: command message

concepts.definition: document message: a message that transfers a data structure between applications.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: document message

concepts.definition: event message: a message that announces something that has happened.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: event message

concepts.definition: request-reply: a two-way conversation: a request message and a correlated reply.
return address: a request tells the replier which channel to send the reply on.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: return address

concepts.definition: correlation identifier: a unique id that ties a reply to the request that caused it.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: correlation identifier

concepts.definition: message expiration: a time after which a message should be ignored if not yet consumed.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: message expiration

concepts.definition: content enricher: adds missing data to a message by looking it up from an outside source.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: content enricher

concepts.definition: content filter: removes unneeded data from a message, leaving only what the receiver should see.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: content filter

concepts.definition: claim check: stores a large payload and puts a claim check in the message so later steps can retrieve it.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: claim check

concepts.definition: normalizer: routes messages of different formats through the right translator into a common format.
canonical data model: a shared message format independent of any one application's data model.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: canonical data model

concepts.definition: splitter: breaks a compound message into a series of individual messages.
aggregator: combines related messages into a single message.
resequencer: puts a stream of related but out-of-order messages back into the original sequence.
scatter-gather: broadcasts a request to multiple recipients and aggregates their replies.
routing slip: a message carries a list of steps it should visit, and each step routes it to the next.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: routing slip

concepts.definition: process manager: a central unit that maintains state and decides the next step of a message-based process.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: process manager

concepts.definition: durable subscriber: a subscriber that receives messages published while it was disconnected.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: durable subscriber

concepts.definition: idempotent receiver: a receiver that safely handles a message more than once with the same effect.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: idempotent receiver

concepts.definition: transactional client: an application that participates in a transaction with the messaging system on send or receive.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: transactional client

concepts.definition: polling consumer: an application asks the messaging system for a message when it is ready.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: polling consumer

concepts.definition: event-driven consumer: the messaging system calls the application when a message arrives.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: event-driven consumer

concepts.definition: competing consumers: several consumers share a point-to-point channel so they can process messages in parallel.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: competing consumers

concepts.definition: message dispatcher: one consumer receives messages and hands each to the right performer.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: message dispatcher

concepts.definition: selective consumer: a consumer that receives only the messages that match its criteria.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: selective consumer

concepts.definition: service activator: a consumer that invokes an application service when a message arrives, so the service stays messaging-agnostic.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: service activator

concepts.definition: messaging gateway: wraps messaging access so the rest of the application can stay unaware of the messaging system.
concepts.source: hohpe and woolf, eip, 2003: messaging gateway

concepts.definition: transactional outbox: writes a domain change and an outbound message in the same database transaction, then publishes the message.
mutex: a mutual-exclusion lock so only one thread at a time enters a critical section.
concepts.source: common concurrency literature (posix threads, java concurrency in practice)

concepts.definition: monitor: an object that combines a mutex with condition variables so threads can wait for state changes.
semaphore: a counter that threads wait on and signal, used to limit or coordinate concurrent access.
read-write lock: many readers may share access, but a writer needs exclusive access.
thread pool: a set of worker threads that take tasks from a queue, avoiding a new thread per task.
concepts.source: goetz et al., java concurrency in practice; posa2

concepts.definition: producer-consumer: producers put work on a queue and consumers take it, decoupling the two rates.
future or promise: a placeholder for a result that will be filled in when an asynchronous computation finishes.
fork-join: a task splits into subtasks that run in parallel and then joins their results.
actor: an isolated unit that processes messages one at a time and communicates only by sending messages.
concepts.source: hewitt, actor model; agha; common actor systems

concepts.definition: communicating sequential processes: concurrent processes communicate over channels, often with synchronous hand-off.
active object: decouples method execution from method invocation, usually with a per-object request queue and a worker thread.
concepts.source: schmidt et al., posa2: active object

concepts.definition: reactor: a single-threaded event demultiplexer that dispatches incoming events to registered handlers.
proactor: an asynchronous completion dispatcher that starts operations and handles their completion events.
leader/followers: a thread pool where one leader waits for an event, then promotes a follower and processes it.
half-sync/half-async: a synchronous processing layer and an asynchronous i/o layer meet at a queueing layer.
double-checked locking: reduces locking overhead when creating a shared resource by checking once without a lock and again with one.
concepts.source: schmidt et al., posa2: double-checked locking optimization

concepts.definition: thread-local storage: each thread has its own copy of a variable, avoiding sharing.
concepts.source: posa2: thread-specific storage; common concurrency literature

concepts.definition: barrier: threads wait until all of a group have arrived, then they all continue.
immutable sharing: threads share data that is never mutated after publication, so no lock is needed to read it.
concepts.source: goetz et al., java concurrency in practice

concepts.definition: work stealing: idle workers take tasks from the queues of busy workers to keep cores busy.
concepts.source: blumofe and leiserson, work stealing; common runtime literature

concepts.definition: copy-on-write: writers copy the structure before changing it so readers can keep using a stable snapshot.
software transactional memory: concurrent memory updates are grouped into transactions that commit or roll back.
concepts.source: shavit and touitou, software transactional memory; common stm literature

concepts.definition: single responsibility principle: a module should have one reason to change, and one audience.
open-closed principle: software entities should be open for extension and closed for modification.
concepts.source: meyer, object-oriented software construction; martin, solid

concepts.definition: liskov substitution principle: objects of a subtype must be usable wherever the base type is expected, without surprise.
concepts.source: liskov, data abstraction and hierarchy, 1988; martin, solid

concepts.definition: interface segregation principle: clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use.
dependency inversion principle: high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not on low-level details.
grasp information expert: assign a responsibility to the class that has the information needed to fulfil it.
concepts.source: larman, applying uml and patterns: grasp

concepts.definition: grasp creator: assign the responsibility of creating an object to a class that contains, closely uses, or has the data for it.
concepts.source: larman, applying uml and patterns: grasp

concepts.definition: grasp controller: assign the handling of a system event to a class that represents the system, a root object, or a use case.
concepts.source: larman, applying uml and patterns: grasp

concepts.definition: grasp low coupling: assign responsibilities so that dependence between elements stays low.
concepts.source: larman, applying uml and patterns: grasp

concepts.definition: grasp high cohesion: assign responsibilities so that the relatedness of a type's duties stays high.
concepts.source: larman, applying uml and patterns: grasp

concepts.definition: grasp polymorphism: when behaviour varies by type, assign the responsibility to the types via polymorphism, not a type switch.
concepts.source: larman, applying uml and patterns: grasp

concepts.definition: grasp pure fabrication: assign a cohesive responsibility to an artificial class, not a domain concept, to keep coupling low.
concepts.source: larman, applying uml and patterns: grasp

concepts.definition: grasp indirection: assign a responsibility to an intermediate object to mediate between others and keep them decoupled.
concepts.source: larman, applying uml and patterns: grasp

concepts.definition: grasp protected variations: protect elements from variations in other elements by wrapping the variation behind a stable interface.
concepts.source: larman, applying uml and patterns: grasp

concepts.definition: law of demeter: a module should talk only to its immediate friends, not to the insides of objects it reaches through them.
concepts.source: lieberherr et al., law of demeter

concepts.definition: composition over inheritance: prefer assembling behaviour from parts over deepening a class hierarchy.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns, 1994 (design principle); common oo advice

concepts.definition: don't repeat yourself: every piece of knowledge should have a single, authoritative representation.
concepts.source: hunt and thomas, the pragmatic programmer

concepts.definition: you aren't gonna need it: do not add a capability until it is actually needed.
keep it simple: prefer a simple design that works over an elaborate one that might.
tell, don't ask: tell an object to do work rather than asking for its data and acting on it outside.
concepts.source: hunt and thomas / fowler, tell don't ask

concepts.definition: command-query separation: a method should be a command that changes state, or a query that returns data, not both.
design by contract: specify and check preconditions, postconditions and invariants at module boundaries.
concepts.source: meyer, object-oriented software construction; design by contract literature

concepts.definition: separation of concerns: keep distinct responsibilities in distinct modules so each can change for its own reasons.
concepts.source: dijkstra, on the role of scientific thought; swebok

concepts.definition: program to an interface, not an implementation: depend on abstractions so implementations can change.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns, 1994 (design principle)

concepts.definition: encapsulate the concept that varies: identify what changes and hide it behind a stable boundary.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns, 1994 (design principle)

concepts.definition: class diagram: classifiers, their features, and the static relations among them.
object diagram: a snapshot of instances and their links at a moment in time.
sequence diagram: messages exchanged among lifelines, shown in time order.
communication diagram: an interaction shown as a graph of lifelines and messages, emphasising links.
state machine diagram: states, transitions, events and activities of a behaviour.
activity diagram: a flow of actions, decisions, forks and joins, often for a process or algorithm.
use case diagram: actors, use cases and the associations that show a system's offered behaviour.
component diagram: modular parts with provided and required interfaces and their wiring.
deployment diagram: the assignment of artefacts to nodes and the communication paths among nodes.
package diagram: a grouping of model elements and the dependencies among packages.
composite structure diagram: the internal parts, ports and connectors of a structured classifier.
timing diagram: conditions or states of lifelines over a time axis.
interaction overview diagram: a high-level activity-like view whose nodes are interactions.
association: a structural relationship among classifiers, possibly with ends, names and multiplicity.
aggregation: a whole-part association in which the part can outlive the whole.
composition: a strong whole-part association in which the part's lifetime is bound to the whole.
generalization: a taxonomic relationship between a more general classifier and a more specific one.
realization: a relationship in which one classifier implements a contract specified by another, often an interface.
dependency: a usage relationship in which a change to the supplier may affect the client.
multiplicity: the allowed number of instances that may participate at an association end or feature.
stereotype: a profile extension that adds domain-specific meaning to a uml element.
lifeline: a participant in an interaction, representing one entity over time.
node: a computational or physical resource on which artefacts can be deployed.
artefact: a physical piece of information, such as a file or package, that can be deployed.
port: an interaction point on a classifier that specifies a distinct provided or required interface.
encapsulation: hide an object's internal representation and expose a controlled interface.
polymorphism: the same operation can have different behaviour depending on the runtime type.
abstraction: expose essential features and suppress irrelevant detail behind a named concept.
object composition: build a type by combining instances of other types that it owns or uses.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns; common object-oriented design

concepts.definition: delegation: an object forwards a request to a helper that performs the work.
concepts.source: gamma et al., design patterns; common object-oriented design

concepts.definition: generics or parametric types: a definition is parameterised by one or more types, checked at compile time.
concepts.source: common programming-language and oo design literature

concepts.definition: mixin: a type that provides methods for reuse by being composed into other types, not used alone.
trait: a composable unit of behaviour that can be mixed into types, often with conflict rules.
concepts.source: schaerli et al., traits; common language design

concepts.definition: abstract class: a class that cannot be instantiated and that may leave some operations for subclasses to define.
computational complexity: time and space cost as a function of input size, often in big-o notation.
concepts.source: cormen et al., introduction to algorithms (clrs); swebok v4

concepts.definition: recursion: a definition or procedure that is defined in terms of a smaller instance of itself, with a base case.
graphs: vertices and edges, and algorithms on them such as traversal, shortest paths and spanning trees.
automata: abstract machines (finite automata, pushdown automata, turing machines) that recognise languages or compute.
concepts.source: sipser, introduction to the theory of computation

concepts.definition: formal languages and grammars: regular, context-free and related language classes, and the grammars that generate them.
concepts.source: sipser, introduction to the theory of computation; hopcroft and ullman

concepts.definition: sorting algorithms: arranging elements in order, including comparison sorts and their complexity bounds.
search algorithms: finding an element or structure, including binary search, hashing-based lookup and graph search.
hashing: mapping keys to buckets for expected-constant-time lookup, with collision handling.
trees: hierarchical structures (binary, balanced, b-trees, heaps, tries) and the algorithms on them.
dynamic programming: solve overlapping subproblems once, by memoisation or a bottom-up table.
greedy algorithms: build a solution by making the locally best choice at each step.
divide and conquer: split a problem, solve the parts, and combine the results.
backtracking: search a space of candidates, abandoning a path as soon as it cannot lead to a solution.
string algorithms: matching, parsing of strings, compression of text, and related sequence methods.
computability: what can be computed at all, including decidability and reductions.
concepts.source: sipser, introduction to the theory of computation

concepts.definition: type systems: static or dynamic types, inference, soundness, and the rules that classify expressions.
concepts.source: pierce, types and programming languages; common pl literature

concepts.definition: memory management: allocation, deallocation, garbage collection, and ownership or lifetime rules.
numeric computation: floating point, rounding, stability, and basic numerical methods.
concepts.source: ieee 754; higham, accuracy and stability of numerical algorithms

concepts.definition: probability and statistics used in software: distributions, estimation, and randomised algorithms.
information theory: entropy, coding, and the limits of compression and communication.
concepts.source: shannon, a mathematical theory of communication; common cs fundamentals

concepts.definition: distributed algorithms: consensus, replication, clocks, and failure models across a network of processes.
concepts.source: lynch, distributed algorithms; common distributed-systems literature

concepts.definition: logic for programs: propositional and predicate logic, invariants, and basic formal reasoning about code.
unit testing: tests a single unit in isolation, often with test doubles for its neighbours.
concepts.source: swebok v4, software testing; istqb glossary

concepts.definition: integration testing: tests that several units or services work together across their boundaries.
system testing: tests a complete, integrated system against its requirements.
acceptance testing: checks, often with the customer, that the system is fit for its intended use.
property-based testing: generates many inputs and checks that stated properties hold for all of them.
concepts.source: claessen and hughes, quickcheck; common property-testing literature

concepts.definition: fuzz testing: feeds invalid, random or unexpected input to a program to find crashes and defects.
mutation testing: deliberately changes the program and checks that the tests fail, to measure oracle strength.
contract testing: checks that a provider and a consumer still agree on a shared interface or message schema.
regression testing: re-runs tests to check that a change has not broken existing behaviour.
performance testing: measures latency, throughput or resource use against stated goals.
test-driven development: write a failing test, make it pass, then refactor, in short cycles.
behaviour-driven development: specify behaviour in examples, often in a shared language, and automate them as tests.
continuous integration: merge frequently and run an automated build and test on each change.
continuous delivery or deployment: keep the software in a releasable state and, when chosen, release it automatically.
refactoring: change the structure of the code without changing its observable behaviour, in small safe steps.
versioning: assign and communicate versions of apis, packages or data so clients can evolve safely.
observability: infer internal state from logs, metrics and traces so operators can ask new questions in production.
concepts.source: sre and observability literature (logs, metrics, traces)

concepts.definition: metrics: numeric measurements exported over time, used for health, slos and alerts.
concepts.source: google sre book; openmetrics / prometheus literature

concepts.definition: distributed tracing: follows a request across services, recording spans and their causal links.
alerting: notifies a human when a signal crosses a threshold or a symptom appears.
documentation: comments, readmes, adrs, api docs and guides that explain how to use or change the system.
concepts.source: swebok v4, software engineering process / documentation practice

concepts.definition: code review: a second person inspects a change for correctness, design and style before it is merged.
static analysis: examines a program without running it, to find defects, type errors or policy violations.
feature flags: runtime switches that turn behaviour on or off without a new deploy.
trunk-based development: developers commit to a shared trunk frequently, with short-lived branches if any.
debugging: locate and fix the cause of a failure, using reproduction, inspection and isolation.
profiling: measure where a program spends time or memory so that optimisation is aimed at real costs.
site reliability engineering: operate production systems with engineering, error budgets and defined reliability goals.
incident response: detect, mitigate and communicate a production failure, then follow up.
concepts.source: google sre book; common incident-management practice

concepts.definition: postmortem: a blameless write-up of an incident, its causes, impact and follow-up actions.
release engineering: package, ship and announce a version, including notes and artefacts.
rollback: return a system to a previous known-good version after a bad release.
canary release: ship a change to a small slice of traffic or users first, then widen it if it holds.
concepts.source: humble and farley; google sre book

concepts.definition: blue-green deployment: two production environments, with traffic switched from the old (blue) to the new (green).
software bill of materials: a list of components and licences in an artefact, used for supply-chain review.
concepts.source: ntia / cisa sbom; spdx and cyclonedx

concepts.definition: changelog: a human-readable record of what changed in each version.
concepts.source: keep a changelog; common se practice

concepts.definition: accessibility: design and test so people with disabilities can use the software.
entity: an object defined by a thread of identity that runs through time, not only by its attributes.
aggregate: a cluster of entities and values with a root, treated as one consistency boundary for writes.
bounded context: an explicit boundary within which a particular model and ubiquitous language apply.
domain event: a record of something that happened in the domain that other parts may react to.
concepts.source: evans, domain-driven design, 2003; vernon, implementing domain-driven design

concepts.definition: domain service: a domain operation that does not naturally belong to a single entity or value object.
application service: a use-case coordinator that drives the domain and infrastructure, without holding domain rules.
ubiquitous language: a shared language used by the team and in the code, inside one bounded context.
context map: a view of bounded contexts and the relationships between their models.
anticorruption layer: an adapter that translates another context's model so it does not leak into this one.
shared kernel: a small, explicitly shared subset of the model used by two contexts in close agreement.
customer-supplier: an upstream context supplies a model that a downstream context depends on, with negotiation.
conformist: a downstream context accepts the upstream model as-is, without an anticorruption layer.
published language: a documented, stable language (often a schema) that contexts use to communicate.
open-host service: a context offers a protocol or api so that several others can integrate with it.
separate ways: two contexts have no real connection, so they do not share a model or integration.
specification: an object that states a business rule as a predicate that can be evaluated, combined or stored.
ddd factory: a domain object responsible for creating complex aggregates or entities, hiding invariants of construction.
circuit breaker: after failures pass a threshold, calls fail fast for a time, then a trial call may close the circuit.
concepts.source: nygard, release it!; azure architecture center: circuit breaker

concepts.definition: bulkhead: isolate resources (pools, queues, instances) so a failure in one part does not take the whole system down.
concepts.source: nygard, release it!; azure architecture center: bulkhead

concepts.definition: retry: repeat a failed operation, often with backoff and a limit, when the failure may be transient.
concepts.source: azure architecture center: retry; common resilience practice

concepts.definition: timeout: bound how long a call may wait, so a slow dependency cannot hold resources forever.
concepts.source: nygard, release it!; common resilience practice

concepts.definition: rate limiting: cap how often an operation may run, to protect a service or a dependency.
cache-aside: the application loads data into a cache on a miss and keeps the cache in line with the store.
idempotency key: a client-supplied id that lets a service recognise a retried request and not apply it twice.
audit trail: a durable record of who did what, and when, for later review.
concepts.source: iso/iec 25010; common security and compliance practice

concepts.definition: privacy controls: handling of personal data, consent, redaction and retention limits.
rate-limit concern: application-level throttles and quotas as a cross-cutting policy, not only a gateway feature.
feature-toggle concern: the plumbing that evaluates flags across the application.
type checking: decide whether a program obeys the type rules, after or during parsing.
concepts.source: aho et al., compilers (dragon book); pierce, types and programming languages

concepts.definition: optimizer: rewrite an intermediate form to run faster or use less memory, without changing meaning.
remote procedure call: a call that looks local but runs on another process or host, with stubs and a protocol.
concepts.source: birrell and nelson, rpc; common distributed-systems literature

concepts.definition: websocket: a persistent, full-duplex message channel over http for bidirectional communication.
graphql: a query language and runtime in which the client asks for a shaped graph of fields from a schema.
schema: a formal description of a data shape used to validate, generate or evolve encoded messages.
concepts.source: json schema, avro, protocol buffers and related schema systems

concepts.definition: data migration: a versioned change to a stored schema or to existing records so old and new code can coexist.
branching and merging: parallel lines of development and the integration of their changes.
code ownership records: files that name who must review a path, used by the hosting system.
